builder_plan.scenario: An agent looks good in demos, but you cannot tell which product tasks it fails.
builder_plan.change: Use the study's evaluation idea to inspect a small set of tasks with human-checked answers.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current evaluator and a manually reviewed reference set.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Agreement with human review, missed failures, false alarms, and evaluation cost per task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: DecompGym: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Designing Decomposition Algorithms
summary: The paper introduces DecompGym, a benchmark that replaces output-only checking of agent-written optimization solvers with a three-part audit: a 60-second execution limit, numerical feasibility plus an LLM-judged method audit, and an objective within 1% of the known optimum; its actionable finding is that reflection (diagnosing the failure before retrying) replaces blind independent regeneration when repairing failed agent code. The cost is an extra diagnosis step per retry, the need for a stored optimal objective per task, and reliance on an LLM judge whose method audit rejects attempts that output checks alone would accept (93 of 108). Failure modes include judge false rejections such as the 'optimal if' pattern (96 occurrences, 92 from one model), missing or suboptimal Benders solutions (48 of 62 failures), and the possibility that reflection's advantage does not transfer to domains without a verifiable optimum.
rationale: The reflection-over-regeneration retry strategy is cheap to implement with third-party APIs, but its measured gain comes from a narrow optimization-solver benchmark, so it needs validation on the reader's own agent workloads before production adoption.

claims.statement: The paper introduces DecompGym, a benchmark that replaces output-only checking of agent-written optimization solvers with a three-part audit: a 60-second execution limit, numerical feasibility plus an LLM-judged method audit, and an objective within 1% of the known optimum; its actionable finding is that reflection (diagnosing the failure before retrying) replaces blind independent regeneration when repairing failed agent code. The cost is an extra diagnosis step per retry, the need for a stored optimal objective per task, and reliance on an LLM judge whose method audit rejects attempts that output checks alone would accept (93 of 108). Failure modes include judge false rejections such as the 'optimal if' pattern (96 occurrences, 92 from one model), missing or suboptimal Benders solutions (48 of 62 failures), and the possibility that reflection's advantage does not transfer to domains without a verifiable optimum.
Reflection converts 66% of retries into successes versus 39% for independent regeneration, across up to ten attempts on 81 decomposition-algorithm instances.
